lines: May, fourteen ninety-eight. A Portuguese ship drops anchor off Calicut, on India's southwest coast. The captain sends one man ashore first: a convict, in case things go wrong. Two North African merchants spot him.
[shocked] May the Devil take you! What brought you here?
[out of breath] We came looking for Christians... and spices.
That's in the ship's own journal. All around him: sacks of black pepper, and painted cotton cloth so fine that Europe would name it after this very port. Calico.
Back then, India made about a quarter of everything the whole world produced.‡

That wealth pulled everyone in. An emperor would apologise for a war, in stone. A diamond would travel from a peacock throne to the Tower of London. And a trading company would raise an army bigger than Britain's.
The numbers on your phone were first written here. Even the English word loot is Hindi.
By nineteen fifty, India's share of the world was about four percent.‡ So how did the richest shop on Earth get robbed again and again... and why did almost every robber end up staying?
The answer starts in a city with better drains than many cities today... and a writing system nobody on Earth can read.

In the eighteen-fifties, British engineers were building a railway across Punjab, from Lahore to Multan. They had a problem. A railway needs millions of bricks, and Punjab had plenty of mud and very few stones.
Then, near a village called Harappa, they found a hill made of bricks. Old, hard, perfect bricks, just lying in the ground.
Sir, there's an old ruin over there. Full of bricks.
[delighted] Free bricks? Splendid. Old ruins never matter.
Sir, there are little stone stamps in here too. With animals on them.
Keep the stamps. Ship the bricks.
According to the archaeologist Alexander Cunningham, Harappa's bricks were enough to lay about a hundred miles of that railway. Keep those bricks in mind. They'll be back.
Only in the nineteen-twenties did archaeologists realise what had gone under the tracks: one of the oldest civilisations on Earth.

About forty-five hundred years ago, while Egypt was building its pyramids, cities were growing along the Indus River, in today's Pakistan and northwest India. Together they covered more land than Egypt and Mesopotamia combined.

And they were weirdly modern. Straight streets. Bricks of the same size in every city, for hundreds of years. Many houses had their own bathroom, with wastewater running into covered drains under the street.
Four and a half thousand years ago. Some cities today are still working on that.
In the middle of Mohenjo-daro sat a brick pool, sealed with tar so it wouldn't leak: the Great Bath. Nobody knows what it was for. Maybe ceremonies. Maybe a very fancy swimming pool.

And the people here were doing something that would shape this land's fortune for the next four thousand years. They were growing cotton, and weaving it. Some of the earliest cotton cloth ever found comes from this region. Remember that cloth. It's going to be worth more than gold.
They traded far, too. Their seals turn up in Mesopotamia, in today's Iraq. And on those seals, they wrote. Hundreds of different signs.
Nobody can read them. Not one word. To this day.
Or a grocery list. We genuinely don't know.
We don't know their kings, their gods, or what they called themselves. Oddly, nobody has found grand palaces or giant royal tombs either. Just well-planned cities, built for ordinary people.

Then, around nineteen hundred BCE, the great cities slowly emptied. Rivers shifted course. One may have dried up. The monsoon grew weaker. People drifted into villages, and the drains filled with mud.
So here's the first answer to our question. This land's first great treasure wasn't stolen at all. Nature took it back.

But over the mountains in the northwest, new people were coming. And they carried something they would guard more carefully than gold: hymns so sacred that, for more than three thousand years, nobody was allowed to write them down.

lines: The culture that grew up in north India is known by its sacred hymns: the Vedas. The oldest, the Rigveda, is more than three thousand years old.

Where its composers came from is one of the most argued-about questions in Indian history. Many historians, using clues from languages and ancient DNA, think speakers of an Indo-Aryan language arrived gradually from Central Asia and mixed with people already here. Others argue the culture grew mostly from within India. The debate is very much alive.

What nobody argues about is this. The Vedas were memorised, sound for sound. Priests trained from childhood to chant them forwards, backwards, in pairs and in triplets, so not a single syllable would change. UNESCO now lists that chanting as part of humanity's heritage.
Again. From the beginning. Backwards this time.
Guruji, we've done this hymn forty times.
And tomorrow we do it forty more.
Can't we just write it down?
[offended] Write it down? And trust a leaf?

Over the centuries, these communities moved east into the great plain of the Ganga. They cleared forests, farmed rice, learned iron, and built kingdoms. By about six hundred BCE, north India had sixteen big states.
Society was hardening too, into ranked groups of priests, warriors, traders and workers. Over many centuries, that system, varna, would set into the rigid rules of caste.
And then, around two and a half thousand years ago, a king in the foothills of today's Nepal had a son. A seer warned him: this boy will become either a great king... or a great holy man.
The king wanted a king. So he gave his son, Siddhartha, a perfect palace. No sickness. No old age. No death. Nothing sad, ever.
Then Siddhartha slipped out. And in one afternoon, he saw an old man, a sick man, a dead body... and a calm, wandering monk.
Soon after, he left the palace, his wife and his baby son, to find out why people suffer.

Years later, under a fig tree at Bodh Gaya, he sat down and refused to get up until he understood. When he rose, he was the Buddha: "the awakened one". His answer was a middle way. Not luxury. Not starvation. A calm, kind, disciplined life.
That's the story Buddhists have told for more than two thousand years.
And here's the strange part. Around the same time, another prince, Mahavira, walked away from his throne too, and taught non-violence to every living thing. Jainism grew from his teaching.
Two princes. Zero palaces. Very confused royal parents.
Remember our question about robbers? Here's the one treasure nobody could steal. Ideas. Buddhism would travel from this land to China, Japan and all of Southeast Asia, further than any army.
But armies were coming the other way. Far to the west, a young king from Macedonia had just conquered the mightiest empire in the world. And he wanted more.

lines: His name was Alexander. In three twenty-six BCE, he crossed into the Punjab.
On the banks of the Jhelum river, a local king called Porus was waiting, with something the Greeks had rarely faced: war elephants. Keep those elephants in mind.
Alexander won. And the Greek writers tell a famous story about what came next.
How do you wish to be treated?
Then Alexander pushed east, to the river Beas. And there, his army simply... stopped.

They had marched for eight years. The monsoon rain wouldn't stop. And they had heard what was waiting beyond the river: the Nanda kings of Magadha, with a gigantic army, thousands of elephants, and an even bigger treasury.
The soldiers refused to go any further. Alexander, who had never lost a battle, had to turn back. He died in Babylon three years later, at thirty-two.
But a young man in India had been watching the Greeks very carefully. And he had a teacher with a grudge.

The teacher was a sharp, ruthless Brahmin named Chanakya. He had been insulted at the Nanda court and thrown out in front of everyone. So he untied the knot of his hair, and swore he would not tie it again until the Nandas were destroyed.
That's the oath the old stories give him. And he found exactly the weapon he needed: a young man named Chandragupta Maurya.
Master, shall I bring a comb?
[looking at the hair] And... how long might that be?
[nodding at Chandragupta] That depends on him.
Around three twenty-one BCE, they did it. Chandragupta and Chanakya overthrew the Nandas and took their capital, Pataliputra, today's Patna.
Then Chandragupta did what nobody had done before. He joined most of the subcontinent into one state: the Maurya Empire.

When one of Alexander's generals marched in to take back the Indian lands, Chandragupta pushed him out, and then made a very Indian deal. The Greek general got five hundred war elephants. Chandragupta got the land.

A Greek ambassador who lived at Pataliputra described a giant city with wooden walls, hundreds of towers and a moat. And Chanakya is credited with the Arthashastra, a handbook for running a state: taxes, trade, war... and a lot of spies.
Remember our question? The first great conqueror to reach India from the west didn't stay. His army went home. The one who stayed was the young man who'd been watching him.
Chandragupta's empire was huge. But his grandson would make it even bigger... and then do something almost no conqueror in history has ever done. He would say sorry.

lines: His name was Ashoka. And early on, he was not a gentle man. He fought his way to the throne, and he wanted more land.
In about two sixty-one BCE, he invaded Kalinga, on the east coast, in today's Odisha. He won. And then he counted the cost.
We know this because Ashoka told us himself. In an inscription carved into rock, he says a hundred thousand people were killed, and a hundred and fifty thousand were carried away.
And then he wrote something almost no conqueror ever wrote. He was sorry. An emperor, apologising, in stone.

Ashoka turned to the teachings of the Buddha. He called his new policy dhamma: tolerance between religions, care for animals, wells and shade trees along the roads. He sent monks across Asia, and Buddhism spread to Sri Lanka and beyond.
He carved his messages on rocks and tall polished pillars across the empire. And then, for about two thousand years, nobody could read them.
Until eighteen thirty-seven, when a British scholar named James Prinsep cracked the script, and Ashoka suddenly spoke again.
Sir, it's three in the morning.
[excited] This phrase keeps repeating. "Beloved of the gods, Piyadasi."
[triumphant] A king who's been trying to talk to us for two thousand years.
One of Ashoka's pillars, at Sarnath, was topped with four lions, back to back. You've seen them. They're on every Indian banknote and passport.
And under the lions sits a wheel: the Ashoka Chakra. Keep that wheel in mind. Two thousand years later, it's going to win a contest.

But empires built by one great man rarely outlive him for long. About fifty years after Ashoka died, the last Maurya emperor was killed by his own general, in the middle of a military parade. The empire broke apart.
And yet, India didn't get poorer. The next few centuries would make it richer than ever. Because gold had started flowing in from a place that simply couldn't stop buying: Rome.

lines: Around two thousand years ago, ships sailed from Egypt to India's southern coast, riding the monsoon winds. They went home loaded with pepper, gems and cotton cloth.

And Rome paid in gold. So much gold that the Roman writer Pliny complained about it. He grumbled that India drained the empire of fifty million sesterces every single year. Hoards of Roman coins still turn up in south India today.
Keep Pliny's complaint in mind. Seventeen centuries later, someone in India is going to make exactly the same complaint... the other way round.

In the north, newcomers from Central Asia, the Kushans, built an empire, and their greatest king became a champion of Buddhism. Remember our question? They came as outsiders. They stayed, and became part of India.
Then, around three twenty CE, a new family united the north: the Guptas. And what people remember about the Gupta age isn't its battles. It's its ideas.
In four ninety-nine, a twenty-three-year-old mathematician named Aryabhata wrote that the Earth spins on its own axis. That's about a thousand years before Copernicus.
So the sky turns around the Earth every night?
No. The Earth turns. The sky stays still.
Then why am I not dizzy?
[patiently] I'll explain tomorrow. If the Earth is still here.
Aryabhata also worked out pi to four decimal places: three point one four one six.

And Indian mathematicians were building the number system you use every single day: nine digits, plus a sign for nothing. A little later, another mathematician wrote down the rules for zero as a number in its own right.
Those numerals travelled to the Arab world, and then to Europe. Which is why Europeans called them... Arabic numerals. The numbers on your phone are Indian.

This age gave the world something else too: a war game on an eight-by-eight board, with elephants, chariots, horses and foot soldiers. Chaturanga. Carried west through Persia, it became the game we call chess.

Students crossed Asia to study at Nalanda, one of the world's first great universities. And in Delhi stands an iron pillar from this age that has stood in the rain for about sixteen hundred years... and has barely rusted.
In the far south, the Chola kings later built one of the greatest navies in Asian history, and sent it across the sea to attack kingdoms in Sumatra and Malaya.
This was the land Indians still call, in its richest times, Sone ki Chidiya: the Golden Bird.
And a bird that shiny gets noticed. In Afghanistan, a powerful sultan had just learned exactly how much gold was sitting inside India's temples.

lines: His name was Mahmud of Ghazni. Starting around the year one thousand, he raided north India again and again. About seventeen times.

He came for gold. His raiders stripped cities and temples, including the famous temple of Somnath in Gujarat, in ten twenty-six. Then he went home, his camels loaded. Keep that picture in your mind: India's gold, leaving on someone else's camels.
Mahmud never stayed. But about a hundred and fifty years later, another raider from Afghanistan arrived with a much bigger idea. He didn't just want India's gold. He wanted India.
His name was Muhammad of Ghor. And in eleven ninety-one, at Tarain, near Delhi, he ran into the Rajput king Prithviraj Chauhan.
Prithviraj crushed him. Ghori was badly wounded, and his own men carried him off the field.
Shall we chase them, Your Majesty?
[waving it off] Let them go. A man who loses like that doesn't come back.
Whatever he really said, he didn't finish the job.
A year later, Ghori came back. Same battlefield. A bigger, better-trained army. This time, Prithviraj lost. Rule one of history: if you beat someone, make sure they don't come back next year.
In twelve oh six, one of Ghori's generals became the first sultan of Delhi, and began the tallest brick minaret in the world: the Qutb Minar. You can still see it in Delhi today.
In these same years, Nalanda was sacked, and its great libraries were lost.
And here's where our question really begins. Mahmud came for the gold and went home. These newcomers came for the gold... and stayed.

For the next three hundred years, five different families would rule from Delhi. And they were about to discover that ruling India was very different from robbing it. Especially the strangest sultan of them all.

lines: The Delhi sultans faced the enemy the rest of Asia feared most: the Mongols. China, Persia and Russia all fell to them.

Delhi didn't. One sultan threw back invasion after invasion. He also fixed the prices of grain, horses and cloth in the markets of Delhi, and punished cheating shopkeepers harshly. One of history's first price regulators. A very, very strict one.
But the sultan everyone remembers came a little later. Muhammad bin Tughlaq. Clever. Well-read. Full of big ideas. And with possibly the worst timing of any ruler in Indian history.

In thirteen twenty-seven, he decided his capital was in the wrong place. So he moved it from Delhi to Daulatabad, about a thousand kilometres south. And he didn't just move the court. He ordered much of Delhi's population to move with him.
Great news! We are moving the capital. Everybody pack.
[raising a hand] It's... forty days' walk.
A few years later, he moved everyone back.
Then he had another idea. He issued copper and brass coins, and declared them worth the same as silver.
Within months, people across the land were making coins at home. Blacksmiths, farmers, anyone with a furnace. Piles of fake money. The sultan had to buy them all back... with real silver.
Money backed only by the state's promise. A great idea. About five hundred years too early.

Then, in thirteen ninety-eight, the Central Asian conqueror Timur swept in and sacked Delhi. He took its treasure, its craftsmen, even its elephants, back to Samarkand. The city took a century to recover. Remember Timur. His family isn't finished with India.
But here's what was happening while sultans came and went. The newcomers were changing.
Persian and Indian builders mixed their styles in arches, domes and minarets. The poet Amir Khusrau wrote in a blend of Persian and the local speech, and is credited with shaping qawwali music.
And out of Delhi's bazaars and army camps, a whole new language grew: what would become Urdu, close cousin of Hindi.
Remember our question? They came as raiders. Within a few generations, they were eating India's food, singing India's songs, and speaking a language that could only have been born here.
Far to the south, a Hindu empire, Vijayanagara, was building a capital that foreign visitors compared to Rome.

Then, in fifteen twenty-six, a young prince rode down from Kabul. He had lost his kingdom more than once, and he was looking for a new one. On his father's side, he was the great-great-great-grandson of Timur.

lines: His name was Babur. At Panipat, north of Delhi, he faced the sultan of Delhi, who had a far bigger army... and around a hundred war elephants.
Remember those elephants? For two thousand years, they had decided India's battles. Porus had them. The Nandas had thousands. Chandragupta traded land for five hundred.
Babur brought something new: cannons and muskets. The guns roared, the elephants panicked, and in a single day, the Sultanate was gone. So was the age of the war elephant.
Babur founded the Mughal Empire. He also wrote a brutally honest memoir. And honestly? He was not impressed with India.
Your Majesty, the finest mangoes in Hindustan!
[sighing] No good horses. No good grapes. No melons.
That complaint really is in his memoir.
If you're enjoying this, hit subscribe. We can't promise melons.

Babur ruled for only four years. His son Humayun lost the empire to an Afghan general, Sher Shah Suri, who in just five years rebuilt the great road across the north and issued a new silver coin. He called it the rupiya. The rupee.
Humayun won Delhi back... and a few months later, slipped on the stairs of his library, and died.
His son was thirteen years old. His name was Akbar. And Akbar never learned to read.
Yet he built a library of thousands of books, and had them read aloud to him, every single day.
In fifteen fifty-six, at a second battle at Panipat, his army won him the throne. Then Akbar did something smarter than winning battles. He included people.

He made alliances with the Rajput kingdoms, many through marriage, and gave Rajput princes top posts in his army. He scrapped the jizya, a tax on non-Muslims. His finance minister measured the land and fixed fairer taxes.
At his new city, Fatehpur Sikri, he built a hall where Muslim, Hindu, Jain, Zoroastrian and Christian scholars argued about religion in front of him.
[ringing the bell] One at a time, please!
[rubbing his temples] I invited you here to find the truth. Not a winner.
Not everyone bowed. Maharana Pratap of Mewar fought Akbar's army at Haldighati, and kept resisting from the hills for the rest of his life.

But by the time Akbar died, in sixteen oh five, the Mughal Empire was enormous. Remember our question? Babur rode in from Central Asia, missing his melons. His grandson was as Indian as the land he ruled.
And Akbar's own grandson would sit on the most expensive throne the world had ever seen.

lines: His name was Shah Jahan. And under him, the Mughal Empire reached the peak of its wealth and its show.

He sat on the Peacock Throne, made of gold and covered in jewels. And set into it was a diamond the size of a small egg: the Koh-i-Noor, the "Mountain of Light". Remember the diamond from the beginning? This is where its journey starts.

In this age, India was one of the richest places on Earth. And the secret wasn't diamonds. It was cloth. Remember the cotton from the Indus? Indian cotton now dressed people from Japan to Africa to London. Silver poured in from Europe and the Americas to pay for it.
When Shah Jahan's favourite wife, Mumtaz Mahal, died giving birth to their fourteenth child, he built her a tomb on the river at Agra.
Around twenty thousand workers and craftsmen. More than twenty years. White marble from Rajasthan, inlaid with stones from across Asia. The Taj Mahal.

Now, let's bust a myth. You've probably heard that once it was finished, Shah Jahan cut off the builders' hands, so they could never build anything as beautiful again. There's no evidence for it. No record from the time mentions it. It's a much later legend.
But Shah Jahan's ending was dark enough without it. His four sons fought a brutal war for the throne. The winner was Aurangzeb.
Aurangzeb had his brothers killed, and locked his own father inside the fort at Agra. From its windows, Shah Jahan could see the Taj across the river.
[not turning] Is my son coming to visit?
[quietly] Regards. I gave him an empire.
Aurangzeb ruled for nearly fifty years, and pushed the empire to its largest size ever. But he spent his last twenty-five years at war in the south, and he brought back the jizya tax.

His toughest enemy was a young Maratha leader from the hills near Pune: Shivaji, a master of fast raids and hill forts. Placed under house arrest in Agra, he escaped, as the famous story goes, hidden inside giant baskets of sweets.
After Aurangzeb died in seventeen oh seven, the empire cracked. Governors became kings. The Marathas spread across the centre of India.
And in seventeen thirty-nine, the Persian ruler Nadir Shah marched in and sacked Delhi. He carried home the Peacock Throne... and the Koh-i-Noor.
Remember Mahmud's camels? India's treasure was leaving again. But the next visitors weren't interested in thrones. They didn't come with armies. They came with account books.

items.direction: Narrate this as a popular, witty long-form history YouTube documentary about India. The Narrator is a deep, warm, confident storyteller: relaxed and conversational, curious, lightly funny, with a short comic pause before each punchline and before chapter turns. Chars voices the people in short dramatised scenes (merchants, engineers, scholars, servants, kings, emperors, sultans, officials, soldiers): short, punchy, expressive, following the bracketed style tags. Pronounce Indian names and places naturally, the way an Indian speaker would. VOICE IDENTITY (most important): the Narrator is always the same person: a low, warm baritone documentary host. Keep his voice identity and natural speaking pitch the same from the first line to the last, so it never sounds like a different or younger narrator. Emotion is welcome: show it freely through emphasis, energy, pace, louder and softer moments and dramatic pauses, as a real storyteller would. Never whisper or go breathy. PRONUNCIATION (say these names exactly like this, stress on the capital syllables): Koh-i-Noor = KOH-ee-noor; chheent = CHEENT; Plassey = PLAH-see; Ranjit Singh = RUN-jeet SINGH.
lines: Remember the trading company from the start? Here it is.
On the last day of sixteen hundred, Queen Elizabeth the First gave a charter to a group of London merchants: the East India Company.

At first, they just wanted to trade. And what they wanted most was that Indian cloth. Painted, printed cotton, so popular in England that its names entered the English language: calico, from Calicut, and chintz, from the Hindi chheent.
It sold so well that English weavers rioted, and Parliament passed laws to ban Indian printed cloth.

The Company set up trading posts at Surat, Madras, Bombay and Calcutta. Bombay, by the way, came to England as part of a royal wedding dowry, when a Portuguese princess married King Charles the Second. Imagine getting Mumbai as a wedding gift.
To protect its trade, the Company hired soldiers. Then more soldiers. Then a lot more.
Excellent, sir. And this line here: "Cannons. Elephants. Regiments."
[confused] We're a trading company. Why do we have an army?
By the early eighteen hundreds, the Company's private army in India was about two hundred thousand strong. Bigger than the British Army itself.
Its rise began with a bored young clerk in Madras who found out he was much better at war than at paperwork: Robert Clive.

In seventeen fifty-seven, at Plassey in Bengal, Clive's small army faced the Nawab of Bengal. But Clive had already made a secret deal with the Nawab's own commander. When the battle began, much of the Nawab's army simply... stood still.
One of the most important battles in Indian history was won by a deal.
Within a few years, the Company won the right to collect the taxes of Bengal, one of the richest provinces on Earth. A company now ruled millions of people. And its first priority was profit.
In seventeen seventy, a terrible famine struck Bengal. Some estimates say up to a third of the population died. The Company didn't cut its taxes. It raised them.
In these same years, English picked up a new word from India: loot. From the Hindi lut. Plunder.

Not everyone gave in. Tipu Sultan of Mysore fought the Company with iron-cased rockets so good that the British copied them. In the Punjab, Ranjit Singh built a Sikh empire that kept the Company out for forty years. He even got the Koh-i-Noor.
But after he died, the Company took the Punjab. And the diamond went to Queen Victoria.
Remember our question? Every robber before had stayed, and become part of India. This one kept its headquarters in London.
By the eighteen-fifties, the Company controlled most of India. And the soldiers it relied on most, the sepoys, were Indian. That was about to matter. A lot.
